items.title: The Clock Is Running
items.desc: California generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim. That window can shrink to as little as six months if a government entity was involved, so acting sooner rather than later helps preserve your options.

items.title: Partial Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning even if you were partly responsible for what happened, you may still recover damages — just reduced by your share of fault.

items.title: No Cap on What You've Suffered
items.desc: For an ordinary injury case, California does not cap the non-economic damages you can seek, such as compensation for pain and suffering.

items.title: No Upfront Cost to You
items.desc: We work on contingency, which means we only get paid if you recover money. That structure lets you get legal help without paying out of pocket first.

items.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Los Banos?
items.answer: In most cases, California law gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a claim. If a government agency or vehicle was involved, that deadline can be as short as six months, so it's worth checking your situation promptly.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: California uses pure comparative fault, so being partially responsible doesn't automatically bar you from recovering compensation. Your total recovery would simply be reduced by your percentage of fault.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to cluster in Los Banos?
items.answer: Public crash records show higher collision counts along Rt 152, E Pacheco Boulevard, W Pacheco Boulevard, and Rt 165, with reports tending to peak on Fridays between 5 and 7 p.m. These are simply neutral, publicly reported counts, not a judgment about any particular road.
